Dear Sion

Thank you for your request for information received on 2nd July 2026, concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms and other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough.

Following searches of the Museum's collections management systems and associated records, Amgueddfa Cymru has not identified any furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property recorded as originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough.

Accordingly, Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold recorded information falling within the scope of items 1 to 9 of your request relating to such objects.
For clarity:

  *   We have not identified any objects of the type described in your request as originating from Great House Farm.
  *   We have not identified inventories, catalogues, acquisition records, disposal records, loan records, provenance files, ownership records, photographs, correspondence, reports, memoranda or related records concerning such objects within the scope of your request.
  *   We have not identified any records relating to the identification, recovery, ownership or location of furniture or household effects from Great House Farm.

We note your references to archaeological material from land associated with Great House Farm. However, archaeological finds are outside the scope of this response because they do not fall within your request for furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms and other movable property. We understand that archaeological material is the subject of a separate information request and will be dealt with separately.

Under section 1(1)(a) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, our response is therefore that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold the requested information.

Cofion cynnes,

Freedom of Information Act 2000 Request

Sir/Madam,

I am making this request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

I seek all recorded information held concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms and other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, including any and all items we received from Bute Estate, Cardiff Castle, Cardiff Council.  Weather it be museums, archives or any other public body. I know museums have artifacts from our land in Llandough.

Specifically, I request copies of all:

  1.  Inventories, catalogues and asset registers.
  2.  Acquisition, disposal, loan and transfer records.
  3.  Provenance files and ownership records.
  4.  Photographs of items identified as originating from Great House Farm.
  5.  Correspondence concerning the identification, recovery, ownership or location of such items.
  6.  Internal reports, legal advice and memoranda relating to Great House Farm furniture or household effects.
  7.  Correspondence mentioning the Buckler or Williams families in connection with these items.
  8.  Records concerning any efforts by Cardiff Council or Cardiff Castle to trace, recover or secure items believed to have originated from Great House Farm.
  9.  Correspondence with the Bute Estate, museums, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, the Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art and Objects of Cultural Interest (RCEWA), Arts Council England or any other public authority regarding objects from Great House Farm.

For context, I am allegeing that my family was unlawfully dispossessed of Great House Farm through fraud, and that furniture and other historic possessions belonging to the family were consequently dispersed. It's possible the bailiffs from BP were also SAS soldiers. We are still gathering actionable intelligence.

I appreciate that the Freedom of Information Act does not require the authority to determine the merits of that allegation. However, it is directly relevant to understanding why I seek the recorded information.

I am currently developing a full-scale replica of Great House Farm in Patagonia, Argentina as a museum dedicated to preserving the history of the house, its occupants and its contents. Should records identify surviving items from the farm, whether held by Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle, museums or other public institutions, I intend to pursue their lawful return or transfer so they may ultimately be reunited with the reconstructed Great House Farm museum. This statement is provided solely as context for my request and does not seek a determination under the Freedom of Information Act.

If any information is withheld, please identify each exemption relied upon and explain why it applies, including the outcome of any public interest test where required.

If another public authority is more likely to hold the requested information, I would be grateful if you would transfer the request or advise me accordingly.

I look forward to your response within the statutory time limit.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
texts.gm-19fc40e3ff740538:
Dear Dr. Driver,

I hope this message finds you well. I wanted first to offer my sincere
congratulations to you and the RCAHMW team on your recent aerial
discoveries. There is something almost magical about the way a sustained
spell of dry, sunny weather can strip back the concealment of centuries —
revealing sites of profound historical importance that grass and topsoil
have kept hidden from view for generations. It is a powerful reminder of
how much of our past lies just beneath the surface, waiting for the right
conditions to bring it back into the light.

I write to you, however, about a site whose concealment has not been
botanical, but bureaucratic and procedural. My family’s history — that of
Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan — has been covered
up not by grass, but by what I can only describe, with careful precision,
as a major scandal of documentary disappearance, procedural irregularity,
and the systematic obscuring of a separate legal title.

The farm, which stood beside St Dochdwy’s Church from at least the 13th
century (and possibly as early as 1215), was home to the Williams family
from 1667 and later the Buckler line. In 1876, the Bute Estate severed 33
acres for the Llandough Limeworks. Family testimony, supported by estate
records, indicates that following this severance, the farmhouse, garden and
curtilage may have been treated as a separate legal parcel — a freehold
distinct from the surrounding agricultural leasehold. Yet this distinction,
if it existed, was progressively obscured through decades of litigation,
missing title deeds, and what appears to have been a conflation of two
distinct legal interests.

By the time of the 1987 Court of Appeal decision in BP Properties Ltd v
Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, the question of historical title had never been
judicially determined. The court ruled on possession and the effect of a
1974 unilateral licence on adverse possession; it did not rule on whether
the Williams family held a separate freehold to the farmhouse plot. The
original Land Registry first-registration bundle (WA231076 / WA240304)
remains inaccessible following an FOI refusal. The 1971 Ordnance Survey
records have not been examined for descriptor shifts. And the 1667
transaction deed — a 999-year lease, effectively a virtual freehold — has
never been located.

The farm was demolished in December 1988. A 1994 rescue excavation by
Cotswold Archaeological Trust revealed 1,026 early-medieval inhumation
burials — the largest such population yet recovered from Wales — yet the
demolition proceeded without archaeological condition. The RCAHMW’s own
1974 floor plan (ST 16817331, H.W. Thomas) documented late 17th–19th
century features shortly before the final litigation. LiDAR data now show
anomalous features near the former site that may indicate a far larger
Roman landscape than previously understood.

What I am asking, Dr. Driver, is whether the RCAHMW — with its unique
statutory role in recording and protecting the historic environment of
Wales — might look again at this site, not with a drone or an aerial
camera, but with the same forensic attention to buried evidence that your
team applies to cropmarks. The grass that covers your aerial sites is
honest; it can be burned away by a hot summer. The concealment surrounding
Great House Farm is of a different order entirely — it lies in missing
documents, inaccessible registries, and a litigation record that addressed
possession while never determining title.

I would welcome the opportunity to share the full reconstructed chronology
(Version 7.0) with you, and to discuss whether RCAHMW records, surveys, or
cartographic archives might hold the key to uncovering what was truly lost
at Llandough.

With warm regards and renewed congratulations on your aerial survey
successes,

Hywel ap Buckler

On behalf of the Restored House of Williams / Buckler Family Estate

Great House, Manor of Llandough, Cardiff

📞 [phone redacted]

Mathilde,

Thank you for clarifying the search methodology. Your explanation is
helpful, particularly the distinction between records appearing in the
Postal Museum catalogue and records physically held at BT Archives.

Before I proceed to BT Archives, I would like to make sure I understand the
limits of the search correctly and avoid unnecessarily duplicating it.

There are a few further points which I would be grateful if you could
clarify.

*1. Date range*

Was the search for the various names and locations conducted across the
surrounding period, or was material effectively assessed only against the
1897 demonstration?

Could you confirm whether *1895–1900*, including 1896, 1898, 1899 and 1900,
was searched?

This is important because I am investigating not only the demonstration
itself but also possible preparations beforehand and correspondence or
reports afterwards.

*2. Catalogue results which were considered unrelated*

You mentioned that some results appeared for terms including Penarth,
wireless demonstrations, GPO Telegraph Department, Engineering Department
and Williams, but that they were considered unrelated after examination of
their catalogue descriptions.

Would it be possible to provide the *catalogue reference numbers and
descriptions of those records*, even where you consider them unrelated,
together with the reason they were excluded?

I would prefer to examine those references myself rather than inadvertently
overlooking something that may become relevant when considered alongside
other records.

*3. Scope of the catalogue*

You have explained that the physical archives were not separately checked
because the information is recorded on the archival cataloguing system.

Could you confirm whether this means that *all existing Postal Museum
archival holdings, including uncatalogued or incompletely catalogued
material, are represented in the system searched*, or whether there are
categories of physical material which may not yet be represented?

*4. Restricted, closed or unprocessed material*

Were any records identified which could potentially relate to the subject
but which were unavailable because they were restricted, closed,
uncatalogued, unprocessed or otherwise inaccessible?

If so, I would be grateful for the relevant reference numbers and any
applicable access restrictions.

*5. Records transferred to BT Archives*

You explained that relevant telecommunications material appearing in the
catalogue is held at BT Archives.

Could you confirm whether the Postal Museum retains any *transfer records,
accession records, finding aids or other information identifying the
particular GPO/Telegraph/Engineering records which were transferred to BT
Archives*?

If there are catalogue references which would help BT Archives locate the
underlying material, I would be very grateful for those.

*6. The Williams connection*

The purpose of the search for Williams is not to establish that Mr Williams
was a Post Office employee.

The family tradition concerns *a local Mr Williams of Great House Farm,
Llandough near Penarth*, who may have assisted Marconi locally.
Consequently, a relevant record might describe him as a local resident,
landowner, farmer, host, assistant, carrier, messenger, proprietor or other
private individual rather than as Post Office personnel.

Could you therefore confirm whether the search for Williams included
references of this kind, rather than only Post Office employees or
personnel records?

Similarly, were variants such as *Mr Williams, W. Williams, William
Williams and Williams* considered?

*7. Preparatory and follow-up records*

Could the search also be considered in terms of records concerning:

   - preparations for the South Wales experiments;
   - arrangements made with local residents or property owners;
   - visits to or use of private premises;
   - transport or movement of equipment;
   - correspondence immediately before or after the experiments;
   - follow-up reports;
   - subsequent demonstrations or experiments in the area;
   - photographs, plans, maps or other material which might identify
   locations or participants.

I appreciate that you may ultimately conclude that none of these are held
by the Postal Museum. I am simply trying to establish precisely what
evidence has and has not survived, and where the relevant archival trail
now leads.

Finally, if the Postal Museum has any *contemporary publications,
newspaper-cutting collections, photographs, finding aids or other material
concerning the South Wales Marconi experiments*, even where they do not
specifically mention Great House Farm or Mr Williams, I would be grateful
for those references as well.

Thank you again for your assistance. Your clarification has helped
considerably in narrowing the search, and I appreciate your taking the time
to establish exactly what the Postal Museum catalogue can and cannot tell
me.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant) Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare
Professional and Life Member

Dear Mr Haste,

Thank you for your letter of 30 July 2026 (reference N610CGV) and for
identifying the surviving records held in relation to titles WA231076 and
WA240304.

I am not seeking to reopen HM Land Registry’s complaints procedure or to
ask for any previous decision to be reconsidered. This is a separate
request for clarification arising from the additional information in your
letter.

Your letter is the first to set out in detail which first-registration
records survive. It therefore enables a number of factual questions that
could not previously be asked with precision.

First, earlier correspondence referred to a 1971 abstract of title having
been lodged with the first registration applications. That document does
not appear as a separate item in the schedule you have provided. Could you
please confirm whether:

the 1971 abstract of title survives as a separate document;

it forms part of one of the listed items (and if so, which); or

it is no longer held.

Second, earlier correspondence referred to a certificate given with the
first registration application in which the applicant’s solicitors stated
they were “not aware of any question or doubt affecting the title”. Your
schedule identifies the surviving first-registration application as Form 1E
(item 13 for WA231076). Could you please confirm whether that certificate
forms part of the surviving Form 1E, and if not, identify the surviving
document in which it appears.

The purpose of this enquiry is solely to establish what information is
actually contained in the surviving first-registration records you have
listed.

Could you therefore confirm whether those records — including the
first-registration application, the A13/DL list of documents lodged, the
correspondence with Linklaters & Paines, any related applications, and any
surviving examiner’s notes, file notes, memoranda or internal
correspondence — contain any reference to:

Mary Williams (also known as Mrs Buckler);

Fred Buckler;

Ty Mawr;

Great House Farm;

any assertion by another person that they owned, occupied, or claimed an
interest in the land;

any ownership dispute, possession proceedings, litigation, or competing
claim affecting the land;

any issue, doubt, objection, caution, competing interest, or other matter
affecting title.

In particular, could you confirm whether any of the surviving
first-registration records contain any indication that another party
asserted ownership of, or claimed an interest in, the land before first
registration was completed for either title.

If any such reference exists, please identify the document or item number
in which it appears.

If no such references appear anywhere in the surviving records, a simple
confirmation of that fact would be sufficient.

If these questions cannot be answered without inspection of the documents
themselves, please confirm that and identify which specific documents are
capable of answering them, so that any Form OC2 application can be limited
to those documents alone.

This request concerns only the factual contents of the records identified
in your letter of 30 July 2026.

Thank you for your assistance. I look forward to your reply.

Yours sincerely,


Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Dear Mathilde,

Thank you for your further reply and for carrying out the searches.

I appreciate your assistance, but I would like to clarify the scope and
conclusions of the search, as several points remain unresolved.

Firstly, I should correct one detail: the individual I am researching is *Mr
Williams of Great House Farm, Llandough near Penarth*, not "Mr William".
The surname is significant because family history suggests that my
great-grandfather, Mr Williams of Great House Farm, assisted Guglielmo
Marconi during the 1897 South Wales wireless experiments.

I fully understand that the absence of a result within the Postal Museum
catalogue does not necessarily mean that no such person or record existed.
However, I would be grateful if you could clarify the following:

   1. *Search methodology*

Could you confirm exactly which catalogue collections, series, or record
groups were searched for:

   - Great House Farm, Llandough (Penarth)
   - Llandough
   - Lavernock
   - Marconi
   - wireless telegraphy demonstrations (1897)
   - GPO Telegraph Department
   - Engineering Department
   - Williams / Mr Williams


   2. *Scope of the negative result*

When you state that "nothing relevant came up", does this mean:

   - no indexed catalogue entries were found in Postal Museum collections;
   - no digitised records were found;
   - or that physical archival holdings were also checked?


   3. *Records relating to GPO personnel*

You mentioned that most Marconi and Telegraph Department records are held
at BT Archives. Could you confirm whether the Postal Museum holds any
catalogue references, finding aids, or transferred-record information
indicating where the relevant GPO engineering correspondence, reports,
notebooks, or staff records may have been moved?

   4. *The Williams connection*

The question I am trying to establish is not necessarily whether Mr
Williams was a Post Office employee. He may instead have been the
owner/occupier of Great House Farm who assisted Marconi locally.

Could you therefore confirm whether your search included references to:

   - private individuals assisting demonstrations;
   - hosts or local contacts connected with Marconi's experiments;
   - correspondence mentioning residents of Llandough, Penarth, or
   Lavernock?

I appreciate that the absence of a catalogue entry cannot prove that an
event or person did not exist, particularly where local residents or
private landowners were involved.

My aim is simply to establish the evidential trail: whether the Mr Williams
mentioned in contemporary accounts can be identified, and whether surviving
records connect him with Great House Farm and Marconi's experiments.

Thank you again for your assistance. I would be grateful for any further
clarification on the above points before I proceed to BT Archives and
Glamorgan Archives.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler

Ms Longford,

Thank you for your email.

I note your confirmation that Cadw holds no transfer lists, accession
records, archive schedules or other documentation recording whether records
relating to Great House Farm were transferred to the RCAHMW, and that Cadw
also holds no record of their destruction. I also note that the suggestion
that records may have been transferred or destroyed is based upon an
inspector's understanding of historic practice rather than documentary
evidence relating to this case.

However, there remain a small number of points on which I would be grateful
for clarification.

   1.

   The original response of 11 June stated that associated records "would
   have been either transferred to the RCAHMW or destroyed under the Public
   Records Act 1958". As no transfer or destruction documentation has been
   identified, on what evidential basis was that statement made?
   2.

   Does the Welsh Government now accept that it holds no documentary
   evidence that any records relating to Great House Farm were transferred to
   the RCAHMW?
   3.

   Contemporary press reports concerning the proposed protection of Great
   House Farm referred to consultation with other departments and bodies
   before a decision was reached. During this correspondence I therefore asked
   whether searches extended to correspondence with other departments,
   external bodies and related records. Although you have confirmed wider
   searches were undertaken, no such records have been identified. Could you
   therefore confirm whether the Welsh Government's position is that it holds
   no surviving correspondence, memoranda, consultation records or other
   documents relating to any such consultations concerning Great House Farm?
   4.

   Is the Welsh Government's position therefore that, apart from the two
   photographs dated 29 July 1988, no inspection report, recommendation,
   consultation correspondence, assessment, case file or associated
   documentation relating to the 1988 consideration of Great House Farm
   survives?

These questions are intended solely to clarify the historical record and to
reconcile the original response with the findings of the internal review.

Thank you for your assistance, and I look forward to your reply.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

Dear Mr Buckler

Many thanks for your email, apologies for the delay in responding I have been on annual leave. To answer your queries I must refer you back to my previous emails of the 10th 3rd and 2nd July.

I appreciate your concerns and desires to find the information. However, I can confirm that all records were checked for the information you requested and we hold no further information or a record of the destruction. Cadw’s inspector advised, based on his experience, that he understood the practice was to either transfer records to the RCAHMW or destroy them under the Public Records Act 1958. We have no record of any transfer lists, accession records, archive schedules or other documentation recording whether records relating to Great House Farm were ever transferred to the RCAHMW.  The photograph provides the only documentary evidence that Great House Farm was visited by Cadw and did not meet the criteria as it was not included on the list.

To be clear, we do not have any further information which would help with your search for the relevant information. If you remain dissatisfied with this response you have the right to complain to the Information Commissioner. The Information Commissioner can be contacted at:

Ms Longford,

Before responding to my earlier email, please may I add the following to my enquiry, even if you require addition time to respond due to this addition to my enquiry;

In addition to my email of 2 July, there are a small number of further points which I would be grateful if you could address as they arise directly from comparing the original response with the internal review.

The original response of 11 June 2026 stated:

"Any other associated records would have been either transferred to the Royal Commission on the Ancient & Historical Monuments of Wales for permanent preservation, or destroyed under the Public Record Act 1958."

However, the internal review of 2 July 2026 states instead that:

"There is also no evidence that any relevant files have been transferred to the RCAHMW."

and

"It is possible that the file was destroyed before it was ever updated on our electronic filing system."

These appear to be materially different positions.

Accordingly, I would be grateful if you could clarify the following:

  1.  What evidence supported the original statement that any associated records would have been transferred to the RCAHMW or destroyed under the Public Records Act 1958?
  2.  Following the internal review, does Welsh Government now accept that there is no evidence that any relevant records were transferred to the RCAHMW?
  3.  Does Welsh Government hold any transfer lists, accession records, archive schedules or other documentation recording whether records relating to Great House Farm were ever transferred to the RCAHMW?
  4.  If no such documentation exists, on what evidential basis was the original statement regarding transfer to the RCAHMW made?
  5.  Likewise, if there is no destruction register, disposal log or audit trail relating to the relevant file, on what evidential basis has destruction been suggested?

Finally, the original response stated as fact that Great House Farm was visited by Cadw inspectors and did not meet the statutory listing criteria. The internal review, however, confirms that no assessment, report or case file has been located.

Could you therefore identify the documentary evidence upon which that conclusion was based, or alternatively confirm whether the statement in the original response was an inference drawn from the existence of the two photographs rather than from any surviving assessment records.

These points are intended simply to clarify the historical record and to reconcile what appear to be two materially different explanations contained within the original response and the internal review.

Thank you again for your assistance, and I look forward to your response.

Dear Ms Longford,

Thank you for your letter of 2 July 2026 responding to the internal review of my Freedom of Information request (ATISN 27021) concerning Great House Farm, Llandough.

I appreciate the additional searches undertaken during the review and the explanation provided regarding the physical record series examined.

However, having considered both the original response of 11 June 2026 and the outcome of the internal review, I would be be grateful if you could clarify a number of points which appear to remain unresolved.

1. Documentary basis of the original response

The original response stated that Great House Farm was visited and assessed by Cadw inspectors and that the building did not satisfy the statutory listing criteria.

The internal review now confirms that no assessment, report or case file relating to that decision has been located and further states that any relevant file may have been destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.

Please therefore identify the documentary basis upon which the original response concluded that the property was assessed and found not to meet the listing criteria.

Specifically:

  *   Is that conclusion derived from a surviving record?
  *   If so, please identify that record.
  *   If not, please explain how that conclusion was reached.

2. The inspection of 29 July 1988

The original disclosure included two photographs dated 29 July 1988.

Please confirm:

  *   whether those photographs were taken as part of a formal listing inspection;
  *   whether they formed part of a wider inspection file;
  *   whether any inspection notes, recommendation forms, field notebooks, photographic registers or other associated records were created; and
  *   if such records once existed, whether they are now believed to have been destroyed.

3. Basis for the statement that records may have been destroyed

The review states that it is possible documentation dating from around 1988 was destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.

Please clarify whether that statement is based upon:

  *   documentary evidence relating specifically to Great House Farm;
  *   records management documentation such as retention schedules, destruction registers or disposal logs; or
  *   a general understanding of historic records management practices.

If no destruction records exist for the relevant file series, please confirm this.

4. Scope of the searches

Please confirm whether searches extended beyond the registered listing files to include, where appropriate:

  *   ministerial correspondence;
  *   senior officials' correspondence;
  *   legal files;
  *   inspector's working papers;
  *   site visit records;
  *   archaeological or conservation files;
  *   policy records; and
  *   correspondence with external organisations, including the Vale of Glamorgan Council, the former Welsh Office and other heritage bodies.

If any of these categories were not searched, I would be grateful if you could identify which.

5. Welsh Government's position

Finally, I would be appreciate clarification of the Welsh Government's position regarding Great House Farm.

Does the Welsh Government's position now amount to one of the following:

  *   that Great House Farm was never considered for statutory protection;
  *   that it was considered, but the records no longer survive; or
  *   that it is no longer possible to determine whether consideration took place because the relevant records are unavailable?

If none of those accurately reflects your position, I would be grateful if you could explain what the Welsh Government's position is.

These questions arise directly from the original response and the internal review and are intended to clarify the historical record rather than seek the creation of new information.

I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

Dear Sion,

Thank you for your enquiry. I will do my best to check if we have surviving records of this demonstration, although most of the records about telecommunications were transferred to BT Archives so they might have more information than us: https://www.bt.com/about/bt/our-history/bt-archives

  *   Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth, Cardiff (not Great House Farm, Llandough near Cowbridge)
I couldn't find any record mentioning Great House Farm, Llandough. For Penarth, there were some results but they were all dated much later than the demonstration. We have many records on Cardiff, which you can find on our online catalogue Here, but nothing relevant seemed to have come up.

  *   Llandough, Penarth, Lavernock and the surrounding wireless demonstration sites.
Nothing came up for Lavernock either, the locations are too precise for this type of records to have reached our archives. I searched for 'wireless demonstration' and POST 88 Series titled 'Post Office: Wireless Telegraphy and Telephony' mentions such events, but all the files are kept in BT Archives.

  *   Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 demonstrations.
Almost all the files related to Marconi are held in BT Archives.

  *   GPO Telegraph or Engineering Department records concerning these demonstrations.
See above.

  *   Correspondence, reports, notebooks, diaries, staff lists, expense claims, photographs or plans relating to engineers or officials present.
See above.

  *   Any references to Mr Williams of Great House Farm, Llandough, who family history suggests assisted Marconi before, during or after his stay at the property.
I couldn't find any specific file about a Mr William from Great House Farm, but the main records we have that are useful for family history research are the Appointment Books, and the pension and gratuity records. We also have Establishment Books and staff magazines that can be helpful too. Please treat this as a request for recorded information only. I am not seeking advice or opinion.

I look forward to your response within the statutory timescale.

Yours faithfully,

Dear Archive Team,

I am conducting historical research into the General Post Office's
involvement in Guglielmo Marconi's wireless demonstrations in South Wales
during 1897.

Post Office Ltd has advised that your archive is the most likely repository
for surviving historic GPO records relating to this period.

I would be grateful if you could search for any records relating to:

   - Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth, Cardiff (not Great House
   Farm, Llandough near Cowbridge).
   - Llandough, Penarth, Lavernock and the surrounding wireless
   demonstration sites.
   - Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 demonstrations.
   - GPO Telegraph or Engineering Department records concerning these
   demonstrations.
   - Correspondence, reports, notebooks, diaries, staff lists, expense
   claims, photographs or plans relating to engineers or officials present.
   - Any references to Mr Williams of Great House Farm, Llandough, who
   family history suggests assisted Marconi before, during or after his stay
   at the property.

If records relating specifically to Mr Williams cannot be located, I would
also appreciate details of any records identifying GPO personnel, visitors
or local residents connected with the demonstrations, as these may help
establish the historical context.

If another archive holds any of these records, I would be grateful if you
could advise where I should direct my enquiry.

Mr Williams of Great House Farm was my great grandad. I am trying to
ascertain if the Mr Williams post office worker, mentioned helping Marconi
in the article, was the same man as my great grandfather. I am also looking
for any more connections between my family, my former home and Marconi and
the radio experiments at lavernock point. Which I understand were already
underway before Marconi arrived to South Wales.

Thank you for your time and assistance. I look forward to your response.

I am requesting your urgent assistance and referral to the appropriate
oversight bodies regarding serious and ongoing difficulties obtaining
historic records required for my family’s claim concerning Great House Farm
(Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan.

ownership dispute. That is a matter for legal adjudication. I am requesting
assistance to ensure that the documentary evidence required for a fair
legal determination is identified, preserved and made available.

referral through my Member of Parliament. Who doesn't reply. The Llandough
councillor doesn't reply. I follow up monthly and nothing. The council
clerk for Llandough initially refused to cooperate then retired. CADW
initially lied to me too.

After more than a year of attempting to obtain records through Freedom of
Information requests, Environmental Information Regulations requests,
archive enquiries and correspondence with relevant bodies, I have
encountered repeated difficulties which are preventing proper assessment of
my family’s claim. South Wales Police say they don't hold records yet they
were reported by ITV and other news outlets as being heavily involved in
the dispossession of our land and home in 1988. Before our 80p year old
home was abruptly demolished and our land and home since 1667 seized .
Along with all our furniture, artwork etc, originally from Cardiff castle.
Property and reference information

The matter concerns:

*Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr*
Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan

Relevant Land Registry titles:

   - WA231076
   - WA240304

Historic Ordnance Survey references:

   - 38-1-608
   - 38-1-334

There appear to be significant gaps in the documentary chain concerning the
transition from historic family occupation, later possession arrangements,
registration, and subsequent transfer of interests.

My family’s understanding is that there may have been separate interests
relating to the occupied farmhouse/plot and surrounding leased land.
Clarification of the documentary evidence concerning historic title,
occupation, registration and possession is therefore essential.

A key unresolved issue is the evidential gap between historic occupation
and the later registration position, including the documents relied upon
when registration occurred and the subsequent handling of title
documentation.

monestry existed there too and has never been formally even attempted to be
discovered. Its home to one of the largest medieval burial sites, also no
coverage of that exhivation before 20 houses were built on our stolen land.
My nan conveniently died while BP registered our land in their names
in1983. My dad conveniently died after his appeal of landmark legal case BP
vs Buckler 1987 was dismissed and his ECHR rejected and then planning
permission approved.

I'm a former military cyber and electronic warfare professional, in
addition to being my dads son, nans grandson and child from this
dispossession in 1988. Which included what maybe SAS undercover as BP
Bailiffs. Both ripping me from my birthland and demolishing it in front of
us. Along with 2 toddlers siblings and my pregnant mum, who's shoulder they
dislocated while she served them an injuction to prevent them demolishing
or stealing our property.

Fraud unravels all. And the limitation is from discovery not occurance of
it. I alledge fraud. Fraud and consealment. BP should have least told the
land registry we challenged their claim with our claim to the land.
Records requiring identification, preservation and disclosure

Land ownership and registration

   - Application documents submitted for registration.
   - Supporting deeds, conveyances, evidence of title, correspondence and
   internal notes.
   - Any records showing how historic interests were considered during
   registration.
   - Records concerning Western Ground Rents, BP Pension Trust Ltd and BP
   Properties Ltd.

Court and legal records

   - Records relating to possession proceedings from 1955.
   - Records relating to the 1962 County Court possession order.
   - Documents connected with:

*BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2*

Including:

   - pleadings;
   - exhibits;
   - correspondence;
   - administrative records;
   - any associated court documents.

Occupation and possession records

   - Correspondence and documents relating to occupation/licence

   - Records concerning communications with members of the Williams/Buckler
   family.
   - Notices, agreements, applications and internal decision records.

Public authority and heritage records

   -

   Council records relating to Great House Farm.
   -

   Police records relating to events surrounding the property, where held.

   Cadw records including:

   -

   Archaeological records including:

      - photographs.

Demolition records

All records relating to the demolition of Great House Farm in December
1988, including:

   - permissions;
   - correspondence;
   - photographs;
   - reports;
   - decision records.

Concerns regarding record handling

My concern is not simply that some records are unavailable. The concern is
that repeated requests have resulted in responses which:

evidence is preventing proper legal assessment of the claim. I am concerned

within applicable limitation periods.

   - evidence indexes;
   - supporting historical documentation.

I request confirmation within 10 working days that this matter has been
reviewed and that appropriate referrals have been made.

inventories, catalogues and asset registers;
acquisition, disposal, loan and transfer records;
provenance files and ownership records;
photographs;
correspondence concerning identification, recovery, ownership or location;
internal reports, legal advice and memoranda;
correspondence involving the Buckler or Williams families;
correspondence with Bute Estate, Cardiff Castle, museums and other public
bodies.

Therefore, my concern is not that NLW does not hold furniture as part of a
collection. I understand that point. My concern is whether relevant
documentary records were searched across appropriate archival collections
where references to such items may exist.

Mawr/Llandough, I would appreciate confirmation as to whether those
collections were searched for incidental references to:
household inventories;
fixtures;
valuations;
estate correspondence;
transfers or disposals;
provenance information;
references to occupants or contents of the farmhouse.

This clarification is provided to assist the internal review and ensure the
original request is considered in its full context.
I appreciate the catalogue references already provided and look forward to
confirmation of the searches undertaken.
Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sgt)

Ms Daniel,

Thank you for your response dated 20 July 2026 regarding FOI/2026/09 and
for identifying the catalogue references relating to Ty Mawr/Llandough
within the Bute Estate collections.

I would like to request an internal review, as I believe the response may
have interpreted the scope of my request too narrowly.

My request was for:

"All recorded information held concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques,
fixtures, heirlooms and other movable property originating from Great House
Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, including any and all items received from Bute
Estate, Cardiff Castle, Cardiff Council."

I appreciate that the National Library of Wales does not collect furniture
as a category of object and therefore may not hold the physical items
themselves. However, my request was not limited to physical objects or
acquisition files. It sought *all recorded information* relating to such
items.

This could include, for example:

   - inventories;
   - valuations;
   - estate correspondence;
   - fixture schedules;
   - probate references;
   - sale catalogues;
   - photographs;
   - tenancy records;
   - references within Bute Estate papers;
   - records of transfer, removal or disposal.

The response confirms that NLW holds significant Bute Estate material
relating to Ty Mawr, including maps, leases and deeds. However, it does not
clarify whether those wider collections were searched for references to the
farmhouse contents, fixtures, or related estate administration records.

Could the internal review please clarify:

   1.

   What collections and record series were searched in responding to this
   request?
   2.

   Were searches undertaken beyond acquisition files, including within Bute
   Estate papers and related archival collections?
   3.

   Were terms such as:


   - Great House Farm;
   - Ty Mawr;
   - Llandough;
   - fixtures;
   - inventory;
   - valuation;
   - contents;
   - furnishings;
   - sale;
   - transfer;

used as part of the search?

   4. If no relevant records are held, could you please confirm the
   searches undertaken and the basis for that conclusion?

The reason this distinction matters is that my wider research concerns the
documentary history of the farmhouse and garden plot following changes
affecting Ty Mawr/Llandough after the 19th century. Records relating to
fixtures, valuations, inventories or estate administration may provide
important historical context, regardless of whether the physical items
themselves remain.

I am not asking NLW to determine ownership or provide a legal opinion. I am
seeking confirmation that all relevant archival holdings have been
considered and that the request has been searched against the appropriate
collections.

Thank you for your assistance. I look forward to the outcome of the
internal review.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sgt)

Our remit covers complaints where someone believes they've been treated unfairly or received poor service from NHS organisations or from UK government departments and their associated public organisations.

If your concerns are primarily about judicial decisions and potential violations of his rights under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). As the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) does not have the remit to investigate judicial decisions, you could consider the following options:

  1.  Judicial Reviews and Appeals:
You will need to seek independent legal advice about the possibility of appealing the decisions or applying for a judicial review. Legal professionals can guide you on the feasibility of further legal action.
  2.  European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR):
If you believe your rights under the ECHR have been violated, you may wish to bring his case to the ECtHR. You will need to review the criteria for applying to the ECtHR at the court’s official website: https://www.echr.coe.int/.

The EHRC provides guidance and support concerning human rights and discrimination issues in England, Scotland, and Wales. You can contact them for information or assistance: https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/en.

For free, impartial advice, you could approach Citizens Advice, which may guide you on your next steps, including accessing pro bono legal services: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/.

*Editor / Investigations Desk*

Dear Editor,

I am writing to ask your investigations team to examine what I believe is a
significant public-interest story involving one of the most influential
adverse possession cases in modern English and Welsh property law: *BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] 2 EGLR 168* (also reported as *(1988) 55 P
& CR 337*).

This Court of Appeal decision continues to be cited in legal textbooks and
case law. It established that a unilateral letter from the paper title
owner granting a rent-free licence could prevent adverse possession, even
where the occupier had not expressly accepted it. The case has shaped
property law for almost forty years.

My concern is not simply with the legal judgment itself.

It is with what surrounded it.

For several years I have been investigating the history of my family's
occupation of *Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth*, and the events
leading to the litigation. Through hundreds of Freedom of Information
requests, archive searches, Land Registry enquiries, historical research
and correspondence with public authorities, I have uncovered what I believe
are serious inconsistencies, missing records and evidence of institutional
concealment that deserve independent scrutiny.

Among the matters that I believe warrant investigation are:

   - Whether material evidence relating to the occupation and ownership of
   Great House Farm was withheld or never presented.
   - The circumstances surrounding the registration of title by BP
   interests in 1982 despite the long-running dispute.
   - Missing or unexplained historical records across multiple public
   bodies.
   - Whether public authorities have failed to preserve records concerning
   a nationally significant legal case.
   - Whether subsequent institutions have frustrated attempts to obtain
   records through Freedom of Information legislation.
   - The wider implications if a leading legal precedent was built upon an
   incomplete or inaccurate factual record.

My investigation has revealed repeated examples of authorities either
claiming records do not exist, directing me elsewhere, or providing
documents unrelated to the requests made. Numerous archives acknowledge
gaps where relevant material would ordinarily be expected.

I have also experienced what I believe to be persistent obstruction. My
elected representatives have failed to engage despite repeated requests.
Complaints have been redirected without investigation. During my enquiries,
a court employee whom I challenged over contradictory information left
their position shortly afterwards. While I cannot infer the reason for that
departure, the wider pattern has made it exceptionally difficult to
establish an accurate historical record.

This story extends far beyond a private family dispute.

It concerns:

   - whether powerful institutions have been properly held accountable;
   - preservation of public records;
   - transparency within government;
   - the development of UK property law;
   - the treatment of ordinary families in litigation against major
   corporations;
   - and whether historical injustices can remain effectively hidden
   because records disappear over time.

The human story is equally compelling.

My family lived through decades of litigation, uncertainty and eventual
displacement. The farmhouse was ultimately demolished, ending centuries of
family association with the property. Much of my family—particularly the
women—have lived with the consequences for generations and remain reluctant
to speak publicly because of the trauma. My brother and I are now
attempting to reconstruct the historical record before more evidence
disappears.

The property itself has remarkable historical significance. Great House
Farm has connections with the historic Bute Estate, archaeological
discoveries including Roman remains, and local accounts associated with the
pioneering wireless experiments at Lavernock Point during the Marconi era.
Yet the legal battle that made national case law has largely eclipsed that
wider history.

This investigation is supported by:

   - extensive documentary evidence;
   - Land Registry correspondence;
   - Freedom of Information responses from multiple public authorities;
   - archive references from national and local repositories;
   - court documents;
   - historical maps;
   - newspaper reports;
   - and a detailed chronology spanning more than a century.

I have also recorded my testimony explaining the evidence, chronology and
impact on my family: https://youtu.be/XuArB_vYWWA?si=O7TL2i5ocU3vn5fG

I am prepared to provide your journalists with a fully indexed evidence
archive, original source documents, timelines, witness information where
available, and copies of all official correspondence.

I am *not* asking your newspaper to accept my conclusions without question.

I am asking you to investigate.

If my concerns are unfounded, they should be capable of being disproved
through proper scrutiny. If they are substantiated, they raise serious
questions about one of the UK's leading property law authorities,
institutional accountability, public record keeping and the treatment of an
ordinary family whose story has never properly been told.

This is not simply a historical dispute.

It is a story about how legal precedents are created, how power operates,
whether the historical record can be trusted, and whether ordinary citizens
can ever obtain accountability decades after the events in question.

I believe it is exactly the kind of investigation that serves the public
interest.

I would welcome the opportunity to speak with one of your investigative
journalists and provide unrestricted access to the evidence I have
assembled.

*Yours faithfully,*

*Sion Buckler*

2000 (or equivalent records access) regarding my grandfather, Mr. Williams,
who worked in the engineering department of the Cardiff Post Office /
General Post Office around 1897.

Specifically, I seek any records, personnel files, correspondence, reports,
or mentions confirming his involvement in Guglielmo Marconi’s wireless
telegraphy experiments at Lavernock Point (including erecting the 120-foot
pole and related tests to Flat Holm). This relates to contemporary
newspaper reports from May 1897.

Please provide:

   - Any personnel or service records for Mr. Williams in the Cardiff
   engineering department circa 1897.
   - Documents referencing "Mr. Williams" in connection with Marconi’s
   demonstrations.
   - Any other relevant historical files from the GPO telegraph/engineering
   teams.

My full name: Sion Buckler Address: [address redacted], Dinas Powys, Vale of
Glamorgan, [postcode redacted] Contact: [email redacted] Relationship: Great
Grandson

of Great House Farm, Llandough, Cardiff (formerly Vale of Glamorgan). Not
to be confused with Great House Farm, Llandough, Cowbridge, Vale of
Glamorgan. And his role in the Marconi experiment. And before and after
Marconis stay with our family in our home in 1897.

your assistance.

Ms Longford,

Before responding to my earlier email, please may I add the following to my
enquiry, even if you require addition time to respond due to this addition
to my enquiry;

In addition to my email of 2 July, there are a small number of further
points which I would be grateful if you could address as they arise
directly from comparing the original response with the internal review.

The original response of 11 June 2026 stated:

"Any other associated records would have been either transferred to the
Royal Commission on the Ancient & Historical Monuments of Wales for
permanent preservation, or destroyed under the Public Record Act 1958."

However, the internal review of 2 July 2026 states instead that:

"There is also no evidence that any relevant files have been transferred to
the RCAHMW."

and

"It is possible that the file was destroyed before it was ever updated on
our electronic filing system."

These appear to be materially different positions.

Accordingly, I would be grateful if you could clarify the following:

   1.

   What evidence supported the original statement that any associated
   records would have been transferred to the RCAHMW or destroyed under the
   Public Records Act 1958?
   2.

   Following the internal review, does Welsh Government now accept that
   there is no evidence that any relevant records were transferred to the
   RCAHMW?
   3.

   Does Welsh Government hold any transfer lists, accession records,
   archive schedules or other documentation recording whether records relating
   to Great House Farm were ever transferred to the RCAHMW?
   4.

   If no such documentation exists, on what evidential basis was the
   original statement regarding transfer to the RCAHMW made?
   5.

   Likewise, if there is no destruction register, disposal log or audit
   trail relating to the relevant file, on what evidential basis has
   destruction been suggested?

Finally, the original response stated as fact that Great House Farm was
visited by Cadw inspectors and did not meet the statutory listing criteria.
The internal review, however, confirms that no assessment, report or case
file has been located.

Could you therefore identify the documentary evidence upon which that
conclusion was based, or alternatively confirm whether the statement in the
original response was an inference drawn from the existence of the two
photographs rather than from any surviving assessment records.

These points are intended simply to clarify the historical record and to
reconcile what appear to be two materially different explanations contained
within the original response and the internal review.

Thank you again for your assistance, and I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,


Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergenant)

Regulations 2004 (and, where applicable, the Freedom of Information Act
2000), and bearing in mind the EIR's presumption in favour of disclosure, I
would be grateful for one further clarification regarding the scope of the
searches undertaken.

Contemporary newspaper reports from December 1988 indicate that Cadw was
actively engaged with a number of parties during its consideration of Great
House Farm. These reports refer to:

Cadw considering emergency ("spot") listing;
discussions with the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical
Monuments of Wales;
comments made by a Cadw spokesperson explaining why the building did not
satisfy the listing criteria; and
public statements regarding the architectural and archaeological
significance of the site.

press office files, media briefings or press releases;
correspondence with the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical
Monuments of Wales;
correspondence with the Welsh Office;
correspondence with the local planning authority, conservation officers or
other public bodies;
ministerial submissions or briefing papers; and
any other correspondence, whether internal or external, relating to the
consideration of Great House Farm for statutory listing.

The public interest in ensuring that all environmental information has been
identified is considerable. Great House Farm was a site with a recorded
history extending over approximately 800 years, associated with the
historic manor of Llandough, incorporating significant historic fabric
including the coach house and outbuildings, and lying within the wider
context of the Marconi wireless experiments at Lavernock. It had also been
the subject of a 1974 public petition concerning its preservation and, as

consideration for emergency ("spot") listing. These factors underline the

relating to Cadw's assessment survives.

whether any destruction certificate, disposal log or other records
management documentation exists;
if no such documentation exists, whether this is because no destruction
record was created or because any such record is itself no longer held.

My intention is simply to establish whether any further environmental
information relating to Cadw's consideration of Great House Farm survives
beyond the two inspection photographs already disclosed.

Dear Ms Longford,

Thank you for your letter of 2 July 2026 responding to the internal review of my Freedom of Information request (ATISN 27021) concerning Great House Farm, Llandough.

I appreciate the additional searches undertaken during the review and the explanation provided regarding the physical record series examined.

However, having considered both the original response of 11 June 2026 and the outcome of the internal review, I would be be grateful if you could clarify a number of points which appear to remain unresolved.

1. Documentary basis of the original response

The original response stated that Great House Farm was visited and assessed by Cadw inspectors and that the building did not satisfy the statutory listing criteria.

The internal review now confirms that no assessment, report or case file relating to that decision has been located and further states that any relevant file may have been destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.

Please therefore identify the documentary basis upon which the original response concluded that the property was assessed and found not to meet the listing criteria.

Specifically:

  *   Is that conclusion derived from a surviving record?
  *   If so, please identify that record.
  *   If not, please explain how that conclusion was reached.

2. The inspection of 29 July 1988

The original disclosure included two photographs dated 29 July 1988.

Please confirm:

  *   whether those photographs were taken as part of a formal listing inspection;
  *   whether they formed part of a wider inspection file;
  *   whether any inspection notes, recommendation forms, field notebooks, photographic registers or other associated records were created; and
  *   if such records once existed, whether they are now believed to have been destroyed.

3. Basis for the statement that records may have been destroyed

The review states that it is possible documentation dating from around 1988 was destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.

Please clarify whether that statement is based upon:

  *   documentary evidence relating specifically to Great House Farm;
  *   records management documentation such as retention schedules, destruction registers or disposal logs; or
  *   a general understanding of historic records management practices.

If no destruction records exist for the relevant file series, please confirm this.

4. Scope of the searches

Please confirm whether searches extended beyond the registered listing files to include, where appropriate:

  *   ministerial correspondence;
  *   senior officials' correspondence;
  *   legal files;
  *   inspector's working papers;
  *   site visit records;
  *   archaeological or conservation files;
  *   policy records; and
  *   correspondence with external organisations, including the Vale of Glamorgan Council, the former Welsh Office and other heritage bodies.

If any of these categories were not searched, I would be grateful if you could identify which.

5. Welsh Government's position

Finally, I would be appreciate clarification of the Welsh Government's position regarding Great House Farm.

Does the Welsh Government's position now amount to one of the following:

  *   that Great House Farm was never considered for statutory protection;
  *   that it was considered, but the records no longer survive; or
  *   that it is no longer possible to determine whether consideration took place because the relevant records are unavailable?

If none of those accurately reflects your position, I would be grateful if you could explain what the Welsh Government's position is.

These questions arise directly from the original response and the internal review and are intended to clarify the historical record rather than seek the creation of new information.

I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

I request an internal review of the Council's response to my Environmental
Information Regulations 2004 request (reference 00210772).

Thank you for the response issued on 7 July 2026. I appreciate the time
taken to consider my request and the searches undertaken. However, having
carefully reviewed the response alongside the earlier correspondence, I do
not believe my clarified request has been fully addressed, nor do I believe
the response adequately explains the scope of the searches that were
undertaken.

Clarification process
On 28 May 2026 the Council advised that the relevant service area required
clarification regarding the nature and reason for my enquiry.

I provided that clarification on 7 June 2026.
On 9 June 2026 I was informed that my clarification had been forwarded to
the Planning Department for consideration.
Given that sequence, I reasonably expected the final response to address
the full scope of my clarified request. Instead, the response appears to
have focused primarily upon identifying two planning applications and
referring me to the Planning Register.
Those applications are relevant, but they represent only one aspect of the
information requested.

Scope of my request
My request concerns environmental information relating to the historic
Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) estate, including land now forming Church View
Close and adjoining land on the north side of Leckwith Road.

The request extends from approximately 1875 onwards where records exist.
It includes, where held:

planning records;
officer reports;
committee reports and minutes;
planning consultation responses;
planning correspondence;
environmental reports;
archaeological reports;
heritage assessments;
demolition records;
redevelopment records;
engineering drawings;
highways information;
drainage and sewer records;
GIS and mapping datasets;
aerial photography;
environmental assessments;
land-related correspondence;
estate management records;
property records;
archived files;

and any other environmental information falling within Regulation 2(1) of
the Environmental Information Regulations 2004.

Matters that remain unanswered
Although the response identifies two planning applications, it does not
explain whether information was sought or considered in relation to several
parts of my request.

In particular, it does not explain whether searches were undertaken for:

archived paper planning files;
committee reports and minutes;
officer reports;
consultation responses;
supporting technical documents;
demolition records relating to Great House Farm;
archaeological reports held by the Council;
heritage assessments;
environmental assessments;
engineering reports;
highways records;
drainage records;
GIS datasets;
correspondence relating to redevelopment;
records inherited from predecessor authorities;
records transferred to Glamorgan Archives or any other repository.

Adequacy of the searches
To assist my understanding of the Council's response, I would be grateful
if the internal review could explain:

Which Council departments were asked to search.
Which electronic record systems were searched.
Which paper archives were searched.
Whether off-site archived records were searched.
Whether records inherited from predecessor authorities were searched.
Whether any GIS databases were searched.
Whether searches extended beyond the Planning Register itself.
Whether search terms or keywords were used and, if so, what they were.
Whether date restrictions were applied.
Whether any information was identified but withheld.

Information not held
Where the Council concludes that information is not held, I respectfully
request that the review explains:
which reasonable searches were undertaken before reaching that conclusion;
whether the information never existed;
whether it was transferred elsewhere;
whether it was destroyed;
if destroyed, the applicable retention schedule and date of destruction;
if transferred, the destination repository.
Information withheld

If any information has been withheld under the Environmental Information
Regulations, I request that the review identifies:
the precise Regulation relied upon;
the reasons why that exception applies;
where required, the public interest considerations;
whether partial disclosure or redaction was considered.

Planning Register
The response relies upon Regulation 6(1)(b) on the basis that planning
information is publicly available.

I would therefore appreciate clarification as to whether the online
Planning Register contains the complete planning files, including:

officer reports;
committee reports;
consultation responses;
internal memoranda;
correspondence;
amendments;
supporting plans;
technical reports;
conditions;
enforcement material (if any);
archived documents.
If it does not, I request disclosure of any remaining environmental
information held by the Council.
GIS information

The response states that my request for GIS information lacked sufficient
detail.
For the avoidance of doubt, I seek copies of any GIS datasets or historic
mapping held by the Council relating to Great House Farm/Ty Mawr, including
where available:

parcel boundaries;
planning polygons;
historic base mapping;
aerial imagery;
highway extents;
rights of way;
drainage assets;
land referencing;
scanned plans attached to GIS records.
Personal data
Separately, to the extent that any records contain my own personal data, I
request that this element of my request also be treated as a Subject Access
Request under Article 15 UK GDPR.

Closing
I have sought throughout this process to clarify and narrow my request
wherever asked to do so. My intention is simply to understand the complete
environmental and administrative record held by the Council concerning
Great House Farm/Ty Mawr.

If the Council has conducted comprehensive searches, I would be grateful if
the internal review could explain those searches in sufficient detail to
demonstrate that all reasonable steps have been taken. If further
information is held, I request that it be disclosed unless a specific
statutory exception applies.
Thank you for undertaking the internal review. I look forward to receiving
the outcome.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sgt)
Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional & Life Member
[phone redacted]

information relating to the historic Great House Farm/Ty Mawr estate prior
to the 1989–1992 redevelopment—including records connected with the 1938

ownership, occupation, boundary changes, estate management, landscaping,
trees, rights of way, demolition, redevelopment or associated land
management—I request that such information also be included within the
scope of this review.

In particular, if the Council holds any recorded information concerning the
removal of a commemorative tree formerly situated at or associated with
Great House Farm, including work orders, contractor instructions,
arboricultural reports, highways or grounds maintenance records,
photographs, correspondence, GIS records or file notes, I request
disclosure of those records. If no such information is held, I would be
grateful if the Council could confirm whether it has ever held such
records, whether they have been transferred or destroyed, or whether
another public authority is likely to hold them.

that any part of my request has been interpreted too narrowly, I ask that
this letter be treated as further clarification rather than a new request,
so that all relevant recorded information held by the Council can be
identified and considered for disclosure under the Environmental
Information Regulations 2004.

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your request for information about Great House Farm, Williams/Buckler Family, Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan and the further clarification that was received on the 7th June. Your request has been processed under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004.

The Council's Planning records have been reviewed and the Planning department has provided the following response:

In line with your clarification that was received on the 7th June, searches have been undertaken by the Council's Planning department in relation to the historic Great House Farm / Ty Mawr estate in Llandough. This includes land adjacent to and including Church View Close and the north side of Leckwith Road, with particular reference to the area identified within Land Registry title WA231076 and the timeframe indicated from 1875 onwards, where records exist.

We have been advised that the links to the planning records relating to the redevelopment of the site during the 1980s-1990s have previously been provided by colleagues in the Planning department. These records, including associated documentation, are publicly available via the Council's Planning Register and can be accessed using the relevant application reference numbers at View or Comment on a Planning Application<https://www.valeofglamorgan.gov.uk/en/living/planning_and_building_control/Planning/Planning-Applications/View-or-Comment-on-a-Planning-Application.aspx>.
This information is therefore excepted under Regulation 6(1)(b) of the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 - information already publicly available and easily accessible by other means.

Whilst planning files may contain some archaeological information, it is also noted that archaeological records for the Vale of Glamorgan are maintained by Heneb (formerly Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust). We suggest that you contact Heneb directly to access relevant records. Details on how to contact them can be found at Heneb - The Trust for Welsh Archaeology<https://heneb.org.uk/>. To the extent that the Council does not hold further archaeological reports beyond those contained within planning files, Regulation 12(4)(a) of the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 (information not held) applies.

Following searches of Planning records, no additional information has been identified within the scope of your request. You asked whether any records may have been transferred to Glamorgan Archives or otherwise. It is possible that historic material of this nature may be held externally, and you may therefore wish to contact Glamorgan Archives directly. Details on how to contact them can be found at https://glamarchives.gov.uk/contact/.

From the clarification provided, the Council has been unable to identify which specific GIS datasets are being sought. Please provide further clarification regarding this and once received, we will consider this element further.

As previously advised, the Council does not hold records relating to the legal case of BP Properties Ltd v Buckler. Neither the Vale of Glamorgan Council nor its predecessor authorities were parties to that case, which appears to have been a private legal matter. Accordingly, information relating to those proceedings is not held by the Council.

If you are dissatisfied with the handling of your request, you have the right to ask for an internal review. Internal review requests should be made within 40 working days of the date of receipt of the response to your original letter and should be addressed to:

  *   whether those photographs were taken as part of a formal listing inspection;
  *   whether they formed part of a wider inspection file;

  *   if such records once existed, whether they are now believed to have been destroyed.

Sion Buckler

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

museums, archives or any other public body. I know museums have artifacts
from our land in Llandough.

   3. Provenance files and ownership records.

Ordnance Survey Historical Enquiries Team,

I am writing to request information regarding historical Ordnance Survey mapping and naming conventions for a specific area in Llandough, near Penarth, Vale of Glamorgan (Wales).

I am researching the historical depiction of a property and surrounding land historically referred to as Ty Mawr / Great House Farm, and I am trying to understand how its labelling and placement may have changed across Ordnance Survey map editions.

Specific mapping references
The area I am examining includes the following Ordnance Survey historical map references:
38-1-608
38-1-334

I am also comparing Ordnance Survey map editions from approximately the 1950s through to the early 1970s.

Mapping issue being investigated
From comparing available historical map editions, I have observed the following:

Earlier Ordnance Survey maps (pre-1950s / early 1950s) appear to consistently show the name Ty Mawr / Great House Farm in one field or parcel location.

In later editions (circa early 1970s), the label “Ty Mawr” appears to shift position between adjacent parcels, and the descriptor “Farm” appears to be applied or positioned differently than in earlier mapping.

There also appears to be a change in how the surrounding land parcels are labelled or visually grouped.

What I am seeking clarification on
Could you please advise:

Whether Ordnance Survey records show any map revision notes, resurvey information, or internal documentation explaining changes in naming or label placement for this area between approximately 1950 and 1975
Whether changes such as the movement of a name between adjacent parcels would typically result from:

resurvey work or updated field recording
cartographic generalisation or redraw practices
changes in naming conventions or feature classification
Whether OS holds any guidance or archival material explaining how estate names or farm names were assigned, repositioned, or reinterpreted across map editions in this period

Which historical Ordnance Survey editions or map series would best show the most accurate progression of naming and label placement for this specific site

If possible, I would also appreciate guidance on accessing any archived mapping sheets or revision history material relevant to this location.

Thank you for your assistance. I appreciate your time in helping clarify how Ordnance Survey mapping practices evolved during this period.

Kind regards,

George,

Have you had an opportunity to look into any of the concerns I have raised
with you regarding my family's dispossession from land at Llandough?

Might we be able to achieve even the smallest task together in trying to
unravel what I allege may have involved fraud, concealment, mistakes, or
other wrongdoing surrounding my family's loss of possession of land there?

It is land that my family claimed to own, and that claim has never, to my
knowledge, been extinguished or determined against us by a court.

The possibility of errors relating to my grandmother's and father's deaths,
court mistakes, Land Registry mistakes, the dismissal of my father's appeal
against the 1987 ruling, the rejection of the ECHR application, and Cadw's
inaction do not alter the central point: my family's claim to ownership of
the land itself has never been properly adjudicated upon or defeated.

I may even have an interest in Church View Close. I am raising concerns
about what could amount to a major scandal in the manner in which my family
and I were dispossessed of land there. Your lack of response, together with
a number of unusual or contradictory responses I have received from other
parties connected with the matter, has not reassured me that there is a
willingness to examine these issues openly.

If evidence was destroyed, if mistakes were made, or if fraud or
concealment occurred, I am sure you would prefer to assist in establishing
the truth rather than be perceived as defending or perpetuating any
wrongdoing.

Would you at least be willing to help with the more limited task of
identifying when the tree planted by my family was removed? From what I can
gather, the tree planting commemorated our claim to absolute title over our
plot of land. Its removal could arguably represent the destruction of
evidence connected with that claim.

Regards,

Sion Buckler
